# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand encompasses early childhood, primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, largely overseen by the Ministry of Education. Early childhood education is widespread, provided through various centres such as kindergartens, kōhanga reo, playcentres, and licensed care centres, with a curriculum framework known as Te Whāriki. Compulsory schooling extends from age 6 to 16, although most begin at age 5. The system comprises 13 year levels, with primary education (Years 1–8) including intermediate years and secondary schooling (Years 9–13). State and state-integrated schools receive government funding, while private schools operate with higher fees and less government support. The national curriculum (NZC for English-medium and TMoA for Māori-medium) is followed by all state and state-integrated schools, specifying eight core learning areas. From Year 11, most students pursue NCEA qualifications, with some schools offering CIE or IB.
New Zealand offers options for Māori-medium education, including kura kaupapa Māori and immersion schools, supporting revitalization of the Māori language and achieving better academic outcomes for Māori learners. State school enrolment often uses geographically-defined zones, which impact access to preferred schools and can affect local property values. School funding is allocated per student, with additional amounts for smaller and lower socio-economic decile schools. Tertiary education, regulated through the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, is funded by a mix of government subsidies and student fees, with financial support available via loans and allowances. Education standards are frequently evaluated in international studies, highlighting strengths in teaching quality but identifying challenges in numeracy, literacy, and equity outcomes, particularly for Māori and Pacific Island students. School bullying remains a significant issue, prompting government interventions.
